title: Incremental adaptor patterns for compatibility shim across TS/Python/Go SDKs
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: Our hosted API now exposes progressive token/delta events, explicit tool/function calls, and structured output envelopes. TypeScript, Python, and Go SDK idioms for streaming and invocations differ widely: TS typically uses AsyncIterable/ReadableStream, Python uses async generators or sync iterators, and Go uses channels or callback handlers. Customers report friction when migrating to the new structured streaming model because they must refactor large sections of app code.

Goal: Design and implement a compatibility shim (Incremental Adaptor) pattern in each SDK that: (1) exposes idiomatic streaming primitives for the language, (2) preserves typed structured-event envelopes (delta, tool_call, tool_result, final), (3) provides lightweight bridges so older callback-based integrations continue to work, and (4) documents migration patterns and examples.

Non-goals: introducing new transport protocols; full runtime rework; heavy breaking changes to existing synchronous SDK surface area.

Constraints & trade-offs:
- Minimal perf overhead: adapter should add <5% median p99 latency and <10% additional memory per-stream across common workloads.
- API ergonomics vs strict typing: TS will favor strong types and helper transforms; Python will keep protocol duck-typed but provide typed stubs.
- Go will prioritize zero-copy and channel semantics and provide a small helper to convert to a callback API for legacy code.

Deliverables: design doc + RFC, TS/Py/Go prototype adaptors, examples repo updates, migration guide, tests and benchmarks.
acceptance_criteria: Design RFC approved by API and SDK leads
Prototypes implemented for TypeScript, Python, and Go that expose idiomatic streaming primitives
Compatibility bridge: legacy callback-based stream handlers can be attached without code rewrite
End-to-end example apps (chat, tool-invocation, structured-json output) updated in examples repo
Unit & integration tests covering event ordering, tool invocation lifecycle, and error/fallback scenarios
Performance: adapter overhead validated; median added latency <5% and memory overhead <10% for standard payloads
Migration guide with 3 minimal-change patterns and copy-paste examples published in SDK docs

examples_snippets:
Python example:

# async iterator (preferred)
async for evt in client.stream(model='redwood-compact', input=prompt):
    if evt['type'] == 'delta':
        print(evt['delta'], end='')
    elif evt['type'] == 'tool_call':
        res = run_tool_sync(evt['tool']['name'], evt['tool']['args'])
        await client.send_tool_result(evt['id'], res)

# sync helper for WSGI apps
for evt in client.stream_sync(...):
    handle(evt)
risks: Behavioral mismatch across languages could confuse developers; mitigate via clear docs and examples
Performance regressions if adaptors allocate per-event; mitigate with pooling and zero-copy paths in Go/TS
Edge cases around reconnection/resume semantics for KV cache and tool invocation lifecycles
Potential API churn if we overfit to early customer patterns; minimize by keeping bridges thin and experimental flagging
notes: Design note: use a small canonical Event envelope: { id, type: [delta|tool_call|tool_result|final|error], meta, payload }
We must preserve id-based correlation so tool calls can be resumed after reconnects
Consider adding a tiny runtime 'shim' shipped as part of each SDK that normalizes framing and backpressure behaviors
TS will export typed discriminated unions for Event; Python will include TypedDict stubs for mypy users
Go will provide clear zero-allocation event structs and an adapter that can marshal to JSON for clients that need it
